scenario.name: Microsoft Defender TI, CISA & MITRE — Entra ID OAuth 2.0 Device Code Flow (/devicecode) Token Audit
scenario.overview: Imagine a cloud office park that offers a handy short pairing code so smart TVs and printers without keyboards can sign in easily. A con artist walks up to the pairing booth, grabs a fresh nine-character code, mails it to an employee claiming it unlocks an urgent meeting invite, and waits while the employee types the code on the official corporate login page; the instant the employee clicks approve, the con artist receives a master family-of-apps pass that unlocks email, file lockers, and team chat. In this scenario (T1528, Microsoft Defender TI, CISA & MITRE, Entra ID OAuth 2.0 Device Code Flow , /devicecode Token Audit), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: oAuth 2.0 /devicecode Request, then family of Client IDs Refresh Token Exchange, then microsoft Graph API Mail, OneDrive. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering OAuth 2.0 /devicecode Request, then Family of Client IDs Refresh Token Exchange, then Microsoft Graph API Mail, OneDrive, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection pivots on Azure AD Event 0 correlated across the documented kill chain.

specs.value: Block the Device Code authentication flow via Entra ID Conditional Access ("Authentication flows -> Transfer methods -> Device code flow") for all users except dedicated conference-room hardware.

stages.title: Stage 1: OAuth 2.0 /devicecode Request & User Code Redemption on devicelogin
stages.subtitle: Credential Access (T1528 - Steal Application Access Token)
stages.description: Requesting a legitimate nine-character device-pairing code from the cloud lobby, the phisher sends it to a targeted employee inside a realistic invitation lure so the employee unwittingly signs in with their real password and MFA on the genuine company login page. An external client requests a device_code and 9-character user_code from login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/devicecode using a public client_id. stages.title: Stage 2: Family of Client IDs (FOCI) Refresh Token Exchange Across Graph Scopes
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1550.001 - Application Access Token)
stages.description: Because Microsoft trusted family of workplace applications shares a single interchangeable master refresh voucher, the intruder immediately swaps the freshly captured token for brand-new passes spanning multiple high-value office wings without ever prompting the employee again. Once the device_code poll succeeds, the remote client receives an OAuth Refresh Token belonging to Microsoft Family of Client IDs (FOCI), enabling silent token exchange across Microsoft Graph, Azure Resource Manager, and Exchange Online scopes in AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs (logged in Linux Audit Event 0 with LogSource=AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, ExchangedResource=Microsoft Graph , https://graph.microsoft.com/.default, TokenFamily=FOCI Refresh Token Exchange so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). stages.title: Stage 3: Microsoft Graph API Mail, OneDrive & Teams Message Enumeration Audit
stages.subtitle: Collection (T1530 - Data from Cloud Storage)
stages.description: Armed with broad Graph reading passes, the intruder programmatically searches the victim inbox, downloads sensitive shared documents from cloud lockers, and scans internal chat channels for passwords and wire-transfer threads.
